newsitem.title: italy: ALPINE SKIING-STIANSEN GETS GOLD AND TOMBA BRONZE.
newsitem.headline: ALPINE SKIING-STIANSEN GETS GOLD AND TOMBA BRONZE.

text.p: Tom Stiansen won the men's slalom and Norway's third gold medal of the Alpine skiing world championships on Saturday while Alberto Tomba raced a remarkable second leg to take the bronze.
"Me first and Alberto Tomba third -- I can't believe it," said Stiansen of his first career medal.
"No-one would have expected this, not even me."
France's Sebastien Amiez, the first-leg leader, was sandwiched between the two with the silver medal after he surrendered a one second lead to the Norwegian.
"I won't be able to sleep tonight thinking of the five hundredths of a second," said the Frenchman.
"I would have preferred to finish second behind Tomba than second behind Stiansen," he added.
Stiansen, who had been third after the first leg 1.10 behind Amiez, has only won one World Cup race in his career compared to triple Olympic champion Tomba's 48.
He clocked a final time of one minute 51.70 seconds, just 0.05 seconds ahead of Amiez. Tomba's time was 1:52.14.
"I had no pressure because we had won medals already. The pressure was on Tomba and the Austrians," said Stiansen, whose father was a world record breaking speedskater.
The gold propelled Norway to the top of the final medals table with three golds, level with Italy whose double champion Deborah Compagnoni won a car for her performance.

"Another bronze, just like 10 years ago," the exhausted Italian showman gasped after he had got to his feet. Tomba won his first ever medal -- a bronze in giant slalom -- at the 1987 Crans Montana world championships in Switzerland.

Tomba had been 1.50 seconds off the pace after the first leg and hurried back to his hotel, saying he did not feel well and was exhausted. Italian reporters said that he was being attended by a team doctor and had a slight temperature.
The Italian, who captured both the giant and slalom golds last year, nonetheless turned up at the start and hurled himself down the piste as if his life depended on it.
"After going out of the giant, I wanted to do it in the slalom," he said. "I knew I could do it."

It was a vintage Tomba performance -- imperious and aggressive, sweeping up from outside the top six to snatch a medal -- and it bore no comparison with Wednesday's giant slalom, when he looked in trouble almost immediately.
"There were so many people expecting me to do well, I went for it," the 30-year-old said. "I felt sick at the finish. Its too bad I was sick today, I could have done better."
The medal also ended the Italian's recent poor form in Sestriere, the resort where he won his first World Cup race in 1987 but where he has failed for two years running.
Austria's Thomas Sykora, second after the first leg, suffered a nightmare second run and finished ninth.
"I'm very upset," he said. "At the moment, after my injury, I don't have the energy for such a long run."

Sykora has dominated the event this season, winning five of eight races but suffering injury last month in training in Kitzbuehel, but he faded spectacularly after saying prophetically "Anything can happen on the second run."
Austrian Mario Reiter, last year's silver medallist who had been fifth after the first leg, crashed out.
Thousands of fans lined the course, mostly to catch a glimpse of Tomba, and some even had to be warned off the floodlight pylons where they had sought a perch.
The crowd, the largest of the championships which closed later on Saturday, cheered their hero's every move and waved signs, one of which read: 'Tomba you are immortal'.
